summary: Artemis surface habitats and pressurized rovers will run at about 30% oxygen and 10.2 psi, where materials burn more readily, yet NASA's microgravity fire data is scattered across 24 investigations. Skylab Phoenix turns NASA's PSI combustion archive into an SI-powered website. It cleans 1,955 flight-test records into one schema (191 logged corrections), ranks the investigations for each crewed atmosphere, and runs a validated model live in the browser: a droplet flame puts itself out 75% of the time in cabin air but only 8% in lunar-base air, where it mostly breaks apart instead, while just 37 of 1,613 records sit near that air and NASA's PSI tables hold no solid burned there. An immersive 3D story takes users from NASA's Artemis plan to a real lunar south-pole site, a Fire Lab replays fires with burning rates measured in orbit, an interactive dashboard filters every record, and a fire audit of a lunar base labels where each number comes from. SI briefings are published only when code verifies every citation and number. The result shows what the evidence says, how sure it is, and what NASA should test next.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Skylab Phoenix answers one question for each crewed atmosphere (spacecraft cabin, EVA prep, the Artemis lunar base at 30% O2 and 10.2 psi, and NASA's 8.2 psi / 34% O2 exploration atmosphere): what does NASA's flight data say about fire here, how sure is it, and where does the data stop?

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data engineering. A Python pipeline downloads the 24 Combustion Science investigations from NASA's PSI public API, maps every test table to one schema in SI units and logs 191 corrections with the original value (spreadsheet auto-fill errors, "3400%" for 34%, an impossible 0 mmHg pressure, duplicated rows, a GMT-day typo confirmed by NASA's own video file name).

2. Ranking and comparison. Each investigation is profiled from its own tables and ranked per atmosphere by a transparent, adjustable score, with side-by-side comparison.

3. Machine learning with honest uncertainty. A two-stage physics model trained on 261 FLEX droplet fires separates the three ways a droplet fire ends in NASA's data (goes out on its own, breaks apart, burns to the end), using the stoichiometric flame temperature and residence time computed from each test's air. It scores AUC 0.88 and Brier 0.120 on ISS test days it never saw. A 200-model bootstrap gives a 90% interval, and an out-of-data guard says "extrapolating" or refuses to answer far from the flown tests.

4. Fire Lab. A droplet burns in real time by the d² law, with the burning rate and extinction diameter of the five closest FLEX flight tests.

5. Learn 3D. An immersive story from NASA's Artemis plan over a real 3D Moon (LRO LROC/LOLA) to a south-pole site on NASA's 5 m/pixel terrain, lit by the Sun from JPL Horizons.

6. Flames. 127 clips of real ISS and Cygnus flight video, cut automatically from NASA PSI raw video and reviewed one by one.

7. Dashboard and lunar-base audit. Every chart of the 1,955 records filters the others. A three-module lunar base is audited on materials, liquid fires, detection and suppression, and every number is labelled measured, derived, model, assumed, extrapolated or no data.

8. SI layer. A floating "Ask SI" chat shows briefings written by an SI model (Anthropic Claude) from numbered evidence packs. Code publishes a briefing only if each sentence cites evidence, each number appears in it and nothing reads as a safety verdict (33 of 33 pass). The chat also quotes NASA's own text with its source; nothing is generated on the fly.

9. Next flight. Active learning picks the test that would teach the model most near lunar-base air: CO2 suppression of a methanol droplet at 28% O2 and 0.75 atm.

KEY FINDINGS

(1) Above 30% O2, droplet fires almost stop putting themselves out, so a lunar-base fire must be detected and suppressed. (2) Material screening done at 21% O2 and 1 atm cannot be reused for the Moon base without re-testing. (3) NASA's Saffire V and VI showed fabric and acrylic burning at 26–31% O2 and 0.53–0.70 atm, but at one airflow and with no limit mapped; the highest-value flight test is to map those limits. (4) No combustion test in PSI ran at lunar gravity.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It turns a scattered archive into decisions for Artemis habitat design: which materials and fires need new tests, which suppression question is open, and exactly where the data runs out. The clean dataset and the 191-entry correction log are open for any researcher.

CREATIVITY AND FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

We chose honesty over impressive numbers: every model reports its uncertainty, refuses to answer outside the data, and every SI sentence is verified by code. We kept NASA's published Saffire burns separate from the PSI data, and we say plainly what the data does not record (for example, what happens to a droplet after it breaks apart).

TOOLS

Python (pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn), Anthropic Claude for the SI briefings, HTML/CSS/JavaScript with Plotly, three.js and satellite.js, ffmpeg and Playwright for the flight clips and the demo, pytest, GitHub Actions and GitHub Pages.
